citation.title: Modeling Legal Reasoning: LM Annotation at the Edge of Human Agreement
citation.venue_or_publisher: Proceedings of the 2023 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing, pages 9252-9265, Association for Computational Linguistics

question: Whether generative language models can classify a complex, specialised construct (modes of legal reasoning, 'formal' versus 'grand') in US Supreme Court opinions as well as domain-expert human annotators, compared with fine-tuned models.
data: 15,860 US Supreme Court opinions likely involving statutory interpretation, 1870-2014, from Harvard's Caselaw Access Project; 2,748 paragraphs labelled by four upper-year law students (68% 'none'), upsampled with seed terms (25% formal seeds, 25% grand seeds, 50% random). Five random 75/25 train/test splits.
method: Four law students built a codebook iteratively and tracked Krippendorff's alpha weekly (final 0.63); a decision chart was added before week 5. Compared fine-tuned models (BERT, DistilBERT, T5-small/base, LEGAL-BERT; multi-class and nested binary) against in-context prompting (GPT-4, FLAN-T5-large, Llama-2-Chat 7B) with three prompts derived from the codebook (class descriptions, examples, chain-of-thought from the decision chart). Also a simpler binary task (is legal reasoning present). Best model (fine-tuned LEGAL-BERT) was applied to trace historical trends, checked against scholarly periodisation.

definitions.definition: A legal decision made according to a rule, viewing the law as a closed and mechanical system that screens the decision-maker off from political, social and economic choices.
definitions.quote: A legal decision made according to a rule, often viewing the law as a closed and mechanical system.

definitions.definition: A legal decision that views the law as an open-ended, on-going enterprise producing decisions that make sense on their face and in light of political, social and economic factors.
definitions.quote: A legal decision that views the law as an open-ended and on-going enterprise for the production and improvement of decisions

definitions.definition: Residual class: passages not reflecting Grand or Formal approaches, including substantive law outside statutory interpretation and procedural matters.
definitions.quote: A passage or mode of reasoning that does not reflect either the Grand or Formal approaches.

definitions.definition: Optional fourth label added alongside one of the three core labels when the type of reasoning was ambiguous; resolved later by group majority vote.
definitions.quote: A fourth label, “low confidence,” could be added in addition to one of the three core labels if the type of reasoning was ambiguous.

definitions.definition: For the simpler task, any paragraph labelled formal or grand counts as containing legal reasoning.
definitions.quote: We consider any paragraph annotated as either formal or grand as being a paragraph where legal reasoning is present

proxies.indicator: Keyword filter: statute/legislation/act within 200 characters of mean/constru/interpret/reading/understand
proxies.quote: include any of the tokens ‘statute’, ‘legislation’, or ‘act’, within 200 characters of the tokens ‘mean’, ‘constru’

proxies.concept: Paragraphs likely to show grand reasoning (sampling only)
proxies.indicator: Seed terms such as committee report, legislative history, legislative purpose, social, society
proxies.quote: conference report, committee report, senate report, house report, assembly report, senate hearing

proxies.concept: Paragraphs likely to show formal reasoning (sampling only)
proxies.indicator: Seed terms such as dictionary, plain meaning, ordinary meaning, canons like ejusdem generis
proxies.quote: plain language, whole act, whole-act, whole code, whole-code, in pari materia, meaningful variation, consistent usage

proxies.indicator: Krippendorff's alpha across four labelers and three classes, calculated weekly
proxies.quote: We calculated inter-rater reliability using Krippendorff’s alpha to evaluate agreement between the four labelers and across the three main classes.

findings.claim: Fine-tuned models consistently outperformed in-context generative models on the three-class task.
findings.quote: the fine-tuned models consistently outperform the in-context

findings.claim: Fine-tuned in-domain LEGAL-BERT (multi-class) was the best model (macro F1 0.70).
findings.quote: Out of all models, the best performing model is LEGAL-BERT,

findings.claim: GPT-4 given the codebook descriptions reached macro F1 0.22 on the three-class task, 0.48 below fine-tuned LEGAL-BERT; other prompt styles reached 0.34-0.45 for GPT-4 (Table 4).
findings.quote: the macro F1 for GPT-4 with descriptions is 0.22, 0.48 lower than the F1 for the in-domain, fine-tuned model.

findings.claim: Llama-2-Chat and FLAN-T5 collapsed onto one class, inflating recall for that class.
findings.quote: greatly over-predict one of the three classes, and rarely predict the other two classes

findings.claim: On the simpler binary task, zero-shot prompted models were worse than fine-tuned ones and over- or under-identified the class, yet did surprisingly well given the low effort.
findings.quote: either over- or under-identify legal reasoning

findings.claim: Human annotation was itself hard: agreement was mid-range (alpha 0.63) after weeks of training.
Introducing a decision chart that broke classes into guided questions raised inter-rater reliability.
findings.quote: Inter-rater reliability increased after the introduc

findings.claim: Annotators needed weeks of training to reach consistent results.
findings.quote: it took weeks for highly trained upper-year law students to reach a level of expertise

findings.claim: Predictions from fine-tuned LEGAL-BERT broadly matched the conventional scholarly periodisation of formal and grand reasoning.
findings.quote: the historical trends in our predictions converge with the views of Llewellyn and other legal observers

recommendations.claim: Be cautious using non-fine-tuned generative models to replace humans on complex tasks.
recommendations.quote: We recommend that researchers use cau

recommendations.claim: Validate generative model output against humans and weigh cost-performance against in-domain models.
recommendations.quote: Best practices would call for human validation of generative model results

recommendations.claim: Complex or specialised classification still needs substantial domain-expert annotation.
recommendations.quote: substantial annotation by domain experts remains a critical component.

limitations.point: Relatively low inter-rater reliability among annotators even after extensive training, due to task difficulty and ambiguous passages read out of case context.
limitations.quote: relatively low inter-rater reliability between annotators

limitations.point: Prompts were limited to codebook wording and examples; better prompting might raise LM performance, so results may understate it.
limitations.quote: our results for these models may depict lower performance than is possible.

limitations.point: Prompts were not explored beyond the codebook.
limitations.quote: We do not exhaustively explore prompts beyond our code

limitations.point: The historical application is preliminary and covers only statutory-interpretation opinions.

Single domain (US Supreme Court legal reasoning), small labelled set (2,748 paragraphs) with a 68% residual class; the setting differs from organisation classification, so transfer is not shown. Not stated by authors in this form.

LMs were run once per setting (GPT-4 default temperature; zero temperature and system prompt tried without substantial gain), with no repeated runs or reproducibility test of LM outputs reported; the GPT-4 version is not given.
Final labels for low-confidence paragraphs were set by group majority vote, so the gold standard is a consensus not an independent single coder.
limitations.quote: until reaching a group decision through a majority vote.

limitations.point: No instructions addressed to a reader or AI were found in the PDF.
